10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates computing word similarity using dense embeddings, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
embedding_dimension = 8

# a genuinely simplified stand-in for trained Word Embeddings, already covered in this topic
word_embeddings = {
    "king": rng.normal(size=embedding_dimension),
    "queen": None,
    "man": rng.normal(size=embedding_dimension),
    "woman": rng.normal(size=embedding_dimension),
}
word_embeddings["queen"] = word_embeddings["king"] - word_embeddings["man"] + word_embeddings["woman"]

def cosine_similarity(a, b):
    return np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))

print("Vector arithmetic (already covered as a fascinating property in this topic):")
print("king - man + woman produces a vector genuinely close to 'queen'")

for word in ["king", "man", "woman"]:
    similarity = cosine_similarity(word_embeddings["queen"], word_embeddings[word])
    print(f"  Similarity('queen', '{word}'): {similarity:.3f}")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Word Embeddings represent tokens as dense, meaningful vectors.
This differs fundamentally from One-Hot Encoding's sparse, mostly-zero representation.
Every dimension in a Word Embedding carries meaningful information.
Similar words end up close together in the dense vector space.
Well-trained embeddings support meaningful vector arithmetic, like word analogies.
Higher embedding dimensions capture more nuance, at the cost of memory and computation.
Words that appear near each other often share related meaning, the foundational insight behind training them.
Every Transformer-based model relies on some form of Word Embeddings as its first processing step.
Next up: Word2Vec, one of the earliest, most influential techniques for actually learning these embeddings.
